--- title: "Factorial designs" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(knitr) library(tidyr) # tidy data library(dplyr) # data wrangling library(kableExtra) # tables library(purrr) # perform iterative tasks library(faux) # simulate factorial data library(Superpower) # power analysis for factorial designs ``` ::: ## Designs with more than two levels A design with more than two levels means that the independent variable (factor) has three or more conditions or groups, rather than just two as is typical in a simple *t*-test. Research designs can also include two or more factors, in which case they are called factorial designs. Each factor can have two or more levels (conditions or groups). A common way to analyse designs with more than two levels is the Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). When an *F*-test (i.e., ANOVA) yields a significant *p*-value, it indicates that there is a statistically significant difference among the condition/group means, but it does not reveal which specific conditions/groups differ from one another. When the null hypothesis is rejected in an *F*-test, researchers typically perform planned or post hoc pairwise comparisons based on *t*-tests to identify the specific measurements/groups differences. If the researchers have specific hypotheses about certain group differences, these comparisons should be planned in advance. For instance, a researcher may predict that intervention A is superior to B and C. In such cases, the a priori power analysis should be based on those planned comparisons, rather than the overall ANOVA result. In contrast, when researchers do not have specific hypotheses, they may just perform post hoc comparisons to explore potential differences after finding a significant overall effect. These are more exploratory in nature and typically require correction for multiple comparisons. To perform power analysis for research designs with more than two levels, we will (when possible) rely on two approaches. First, we will simulate the data directly with `rnorm()` (independent groups) and `MASS::mvrnorm()` (correlated measurements) and analyze it with base R's `aov()` and `lm()`. Drawing the data directly is much faster than calling `faux::sim_design()` in every iteration, so `sim_design()` is only used to visualize the expected pattern of means. For the second approach, we will be using `Superpower` to both simulate data and perform the analysis. `Superpower` relies on `emmeans` for planned comparisons. ## One-factor repeated-measures design In a repeated-measures design, researchers collect data from the same participants at more than two different time points or conditions. Typically researchers will use a one-way within-subject ANOVA to analyse this study design. Suppose a researcher hypothesizes that intervention A is more effective than interventions B and C in reducing heart rate. To test this hypothesis, the researcher plans to use a within-subjects (repeated measures) design with three levels, collecting heart rate data from the same participants under each intervention condition. ::: callout-note This hypothesis specifies a directional expectation—that intervention A will lead to lower heart rates compared to interventions B and C—rather than merely predicting that differences exist between conditions. Therefore, the researcher should use planned contrasts or directional (one-tailed) tests that align with the hypothesis, rather than relying solely on the omnibus *F*-test, which only assesses whether any difference exists among the conditions. ::: Let's define the parameters for the simulation: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nsims <- 1000 # number of simulations sample_size <- c(25, 50, 75, 100) # total sample size mu <- c(60, 62, 65) # expected means for A, B, C sd <- 10 # common SD rho <- 0.6 # correlation between measurements alpha_level <- 0.05 ``` ::: ### Simulation using `aov()` Before running the simulation, always make sure that the pattern of means matches the expected pattern of means: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sim_design( within = list(condition = c("A", "B", "C")), n = 25, mu = mu, sd = sd, r = rho, plot = TRUE, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_chapter_files/figure-html/chunk_37-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Let's perform the simulations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # For reproducibility set.seed(050990) # Covariance matrix of the three repeated measurements sigma <- sd^2 * (rho + (1 - rho) * diag(3)) # Perform simulations simulate_power <- function(n) { p_values <- replicate(nsims, { x <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = n, mu = mu, Sigma = sigma) df <- data.frame( id = factor(rep(seq_len(n), times = 3)), condition = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = n)), y = as.vector(x) ) summary(aov(y ~ condition + Error(id), df))[["Error: Within"]][[1]][1, "Pr(>F)"] }) mean(p_values < alpha_level) } # Run for all sample sizes power_results <- tibble( N = sample_size, power = map_dbl(sample_size, simulate_power) ) # Return proportion of significant p-values power_results |> kable(digits = 2) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
N power
25 0.67
50 0.96
75 0.99
100 1.00
````` ::: ::: The above simulation provides power estimates only for the overall *F*-test, which tests the null hypothesis that the three conditions are equal. However, in our example the researcher had a specific expected pattern of means (A \< B and A \< C). Since the hypothesis of interest concerns a specific set of pairwise comparisons, the researcher should ensure that both comparisons are adequately powered. Pairwise comparisons can be tested using `Superpower.` ### Simulation using `Superpower` Let's define the study design: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} design_result <- ANOVA_design( design = "3w", # study design (i.e., three within-subject measurements) n = 50, mu = mu, sd = sd, r = rho, labelnames = c("group", "A", "B", "C"), plot = TRUE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_chapter_files/figure-html/chunk_39-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Setting `ANOVA_design(plot = TRUE)` returns a plot of the condition means, which is useful for verifying that the intended pattern of means has been specified correctly. Now let's run the simulations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Run simulation simulation_result <- ANOVA_power( design_result, alpha_level = alpha_level, nsims = nsims, verbose = FALSE, seed = 050990) # for reproducibility ``` ::: The power calculation of the omnibus *F*-test: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simulation_result$main_results |> kable(digits = 2) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
power effect_size
anova_group 95.3 0.15
````` ::: ::: Note that the achieved power is almost identical to the power achieved using `aov()`. The power calculation of the pairwise comparisons: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simulation_result$pc_results |> kable(digits = 2) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
power effect_size
p_group_A_group_B 35.9 0.23
p_group_A_group_C 97.7 0.57
p_group_B_group_C 64.2 0.34
````` ::: ::: Although the *F*-test has adequate power to reject the null hypothesis of no difference across conditions (i.e., power = 95.3%), only the pairwise comparison between interventions A and C has adequate power (i.e., power = 97.7%). Because the difference in heart rate between A and C is larger than that between A and B, the pairwise comparison test for A vs C achieves higher power for any given sample size. Therefore, a larger sample size would be needed to attain comparable power for the A vs B comparison. ## One-factor between-subject design In a between-subject factorial design researchers collect data from participants that were assigned to more than two different groups. Typically researchers will analyse this study design with a one-way between-subject ANOVA. Suppose a researcher aims to compare the effectiveness of two doses against a placebo by randomly assigning participants to one of three intervention groups. The intervention will be considered effective if **any** of the two doses result in a significantly reduced heart rate compared to the placebo. Because this involves two multiple comparisons, appropriate adjustments for multiple testing are required in the analysis (i.e., 0.05/2), and these adjustments must be incorporated into the power analysis. Let's define the parameters of the simulation: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Set parameters nsims <- 1000 # number of simulations sample_size <- c(50, 100, 150) # sample size per group mu <- c(60, 62, 64) # expected group means sd <- 10 # common SD ``` ::: ### Simulation using `lm()` Let's define the study design: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sim_design( between = list(dose = c("high", "medium", "placebo")), n = 50, mu = mu, sd = sd, plot = TRUE, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_chapter_files/figure-html/chunk_44-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Let's perform the simulations with this expected pattern of means: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # For reproducibility set.seed(050990) # Perform simulations simulate_power <- function(n) { # Placebo is the reference level, so the coefficients are dose - placebo dose <- factor(rep(c("high", "medium", "placebo"), each = n), levels = c("placebo", "high", "medium")) p_values <- replicate(nsims, { y <- rnorm(3 * n, mean = rep(mu, each = n), sd = sd) model <- lm(y ~ dose) coefs <- summary(model)$coefficients # P-value of the overall F-test f <- summary(model)$fstatistic overall_p <- pf(f["value"], f["numdf"], f["dendf"], lower.tail = FALSE) # Unadjusted p-values of the comparisons against placebo c( overall = unname(overall_p), "high - placebo" = coefs["dosehigh", "Pr(>|t|)"], "medium - placebo" = coefs["dosemedium", "Pr(>|t|)"] ) }) # p_values is 3 x nsims matrix, calculate proportion significant tibble( comparison = c("overall F-test", "high - placebo", "medium - placebo"), power = c( mean(p_values[1, ] < 0.05), mean(p_values[2, ] < 0.05/2), mean(p_values[3, ] < 0.05/2) ), N = n ) } power_results <- map_dfr(sample_size, simulate_power) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-power-ftest .cell tbl-cap='Power for F-test'} ```{.r .cell-code} power_results %>% filter(comparison == "overall F-test") %>% select(N, power) %>% kable(digits = 2) %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
N power
50 0.40
100 0.72
150 0.87
````` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-power-high-placebo .cell tbl-cap='Power for high dose vs. placebo'} ```{.r .cell-code} power_results %>% filter(comparison == "high - placebo") %>% select(N, power) %>% kable(digits = 2) %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
N power
50 0.38
100 0.72
150 0.88
````` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-power-medium-placebo .cell tbl-cap='Power for medium dose vs. placebo'} ```{.r .cell-code} power_results %>% filter(comparison == "medium - placebo") %>% select(N, power) %>% kable(digits = 2) %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
N power
50 0.11
100 0.21
150 0.30
````` ::: ::: ### Simulation using `Superpower` Let's define the study design: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} design_result <- ANOVA_design( design = "3b", # study design (i.e., three between-subject groups) n = 50, # sample size per group mu = mu, sd = sd, labelnames = c("dose", "high", "medium", "placebo"), plot = TRUE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_chapter_files/figure-html/chunk_49-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Now let's perform the simulations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simulation_result <- ANOVA_power( design_result, alpha_level = 0.05/2, # Bonferroni correction for two comparisons nsims = nsims, verbose = FALSE, seed = 050990 ) ``` ::: The power calculation of the omnibus *F*-test: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simulation_result$main_results |> kable(digits = 2) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
power effect_size
anova_dose 32.6 0.04
````` ::: ::: `Superpower` evaluates all tests at the same `alpha_level`, so we set it to 0.05/2 to apply the Bonferroni correction for the two comparisons against placebo. As a consequence, the omnibus *F*-test is also evaluated at $\alpha$ = 0.025 and its power is lower than in the `lm()`-based simulation above. The pairwise power estimates for the comparisons against placebo are close to those obtained above (the remaining differences reflect Monte Carlo error). The power calculation of the pairwise comparisons: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simulation_result$pc_results |> kable(digits = 2) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
power effect_size
p_dose_high_dose_medium 11.1 0.21
p_dose_high_dose_placebo 42.3 0.41
p_dose_medium_dose_placebo 10.8 0.21
````` ::: ::: Now suppose a researcher hypothesizes that intervention A is more effective than Intervention B, and intervention B is more effective than intervention C in reducing heart rate. This directional hypothesis can be tested by specifying a set of custom contrasts—that is, testing linear combinations of group means that reflect the predicted order (A \> B \> C). To evaluate this hypothesis, the researcher plans to use a between-subjects design, randomly assigning participants to three independent groups, each receiving one of the three interventions. Planned contrasts will then be used to test the specific pattern of differences. Let's define the parameters of the simulation and plot the expected pattern of means: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Set parameters nsims <- 1000 # number of simulations n <- 50 # sample size per group mu <- c(66, 68, 70) # expected group means sd <- 10 # common SD alpha_level <- 0.05 # Show pattern of means dat <- sim_design( between = list(intervention = c("A", "B", "C")), n = n, mu = mu, sd = sd, plot = TRUE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_chapter_files/figure-html/chunk_53-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: To reflect the hypothesis that effectiveness decreases from intervention A to B to C (i.e., heart rate increases from A to B to C), the contrast weights can be specified as –1, 0, and +1, respectively. This linear contrast tests whether there is a monotonic increase in heart rate across the three groups in the hypothesized order. Result of power calculation for the linear contrast: ::: {#tbl-power-linear .cell tbl-cap='Power for linear contrast (A < B < C)'} ```{.r .cell-code} # For reproducibility set.seed(050990) # Perform simulations simulate_power <- function(n) { # Linear contrast weights: A = -1, B = 0, C = +1 w <- c(-1, 0, 1) p_values <- replicate(nsims, { y <- matrix(rnorm(3 * n, mean = rep(mu, each = n), sd = sd), ncol = 3) # Contrast estimate and its standard error based on the pooled variance # (the same test as emmeans::contrast() in a one-way between-subject design) mse <- mean(apply(y, 2, var)) t_value <- sum(w * colMeans(y)) / sqrt(mse * sum(w^2) / n) 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = 3 * (n - 1)) }) # Return proportion of significant p-values mean(p_values < alpha_level) } # Run for all sample sizes power_results <- tibble( N = sample_size, power = map_dbl(sample_size, simulate_power) ) # Print formatted table power_results |> kable(digits = 2) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
N power
50 0.48
100 0.81
150 0.93
````` ::: ::: ## Two-factor repeated-measures design In a two-way repeated-measures factorial design, researchers collect data from the same participants under all combinations of two within-subject factors. This means each participant is exposed to every level of both factors, allowing researchers to examine main effects and interactions. Suppose a researcher hypothesizes that intervention A is more effective than intervention B in reducing heart rate, but that the effectiveness of intervention A will be increased in the morning compared to the evening. The researcher is specifically interested in: - Comparing whether intervention A is superior to B both in the morning and evening; and - Comparing whether the effect of the intervention A is superior in the morning vs. evening Let's define the parameters of the simulation and plot the expected pattern of means: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Set parameters nsims <- 1000 # number of simulations mu <- c(61, 63, 68, 68) # means n <- 105 # sample size sd <- 10 # SD r <- 0.5 # correlation between measurements string = "2w*2w" # study design (i.e., two within-subject factors) alpha_level <- 0.05 design_result <- ANOVA_design( design = string, n = n, mu = mu, sd = sd, r = r, plot = TRUE, labelnames = c("intervention", "A", "B", "time", "morning", "evening")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_chapter_files/figure-html/chunk_55-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Let's perform the simulations with this expected pattern of means: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simulation_result <- ANOVA_power( design_result, alpha_level = alpha_level, nsims = nsims, verbose = FALSE, seed = 050990) ``` ::: Result of power calculation for the main effects and the interaction effect: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simulation_result$main_results |> kable() |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
power effect_size
anova_intervention 100.0 0.4199987
anova_time 31.9 0.0296104
anova_intervention:time 32.6 0.0300462
````` ::: ::: The current design provides adequate statistical power **(**\> 80%) to detect the main effect of the intervention, but not the main effect of time or the interaction between intervention and time. Result of power calculation for the planned pairwise comparisons: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pwc <- simulation_result$pc_results[c(1, 2 , 5),1:2] pwc |> kable() |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
power effect_size
p_intervention_A_time_morning_intervention_A_time_evening 56.0 0.2073987
p_intervention_A_time_morning_intervention_B_time_morning 100.0 0.7106602
p_intervention_A_time_evening_intervention_B_time_evening 99.9 0.4998926
````` ::: ::: The study design would achieve a power of 56% to test the comparison of intervention A between morning and evening, a power of 100% to test for the comparison between interventions A and B in the morning and a power of 99.9% to test for the comparison between interventions A and B in the evening. Because the difference for intervention A between morning and evening (2 bpm) is much smaller than the differences between interventions (7 and 5 bpm), the first comparison is the one that falls short of 80% power, and the researcher should consider increasing the sample size to adequately power it. ## Two-factor mixed design In a two-factor mixed design (i.e., one between- and one within-subject factor), researchers collect data from participants who were assigned to independent groups (a between-subject factor) and also measured on multiple occasions or conditions (a within-subject factor). This design combines both within- and between-subject factors. When the within-subject factor involves measurements before and after an intervention, the design is specifically referred to as a split-plot design. In interventions following a split-plot design, it is crucial to account for baseline differences between groups. The most effective way to do this is by including baseline covariates, such as pre-intervention scores, in the analysis model. This approach adjusts the post-intervention outcome for initial differences, thereby yielding a more accurate estimate of the intervention effect and increasing power. While several models have been proposed for analyzing split-plot designs—such as comparing difference scores between groups or testing interaction effects—there is broad consensus that including the pre-intervention scores as a covariate is the most appropriate method. Including baseline scores as a covariate improves the precision of group comparisons by explaining part of the error variance and thus increasing power. Suppose a researcher hypothesizes that intervention A is more effective than intervention B in reducing heart rate. To test this hypothesis, participants are assigned to either intervention A or intervention B (between-subjects factor: intervention type). Heart rate is measured both before and after the intervention (within-subjects factor: time), allowing the researcher to assess intervention effects over time. The primary test of interest is the interaction effect between intervention type and time, which indicates whether the change in heart rate differs between the two interventions. Let's define the parameters: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nsims <- 1000 # number of simulations sample_size <- c(25, 50, 100, 150) # sample size per group mu <- c(64, 60, 64, 64) # means for A_pre, A_post, B_pre, B_post sd <- 10 # common SD rho <- 0.7 # correlation between measurements alpha_level <- 0.05 # alpha level ``` ::: Let's visualize the pattern of means: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sim_design( within = list(time = c("pre", "post")), between = list(intervention = c("A", "B")), n = 50, mu = mu, sd = sd, r = rho, plot = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_chapter_files/figure-html/chunk_60-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Simulation using `lm()` including the baseline score as a covariate ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Ensure reproducibility set.seed(050990) # Covariance matrix of the pre and post measurements sigma <- sd^2 * (rho + (1 - rho) * diag(2)) # Power simulation function simulate_power <- function(n) { # B is the reference level intervention <- factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = n), levels = c("B", "A")) p_values <- replicate(nsims, { x_A <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = n, mu = mu[1:2], Sigma = sigma) # A_pre, A_post x_B <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = n, mu = mu[3:4], Sigma = sigma) # B_pre, B_post pre <- c(x_A[, 1], x_B[, 1]) post <- c(x_A[, 2], x_B[, 2]) summary(lm(post ~ intervention + pre))$coefficients["interventionA", "Pr(>|t|)"] }) mean(p_values < alpha_level) } # Run function for all sample sizes power_results <- tibble( n = sample_size, power = map_dbl(sample_size, simulate_power) ) # Return proportion of significant p-values power_results |> kable(digits = 2) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
n power
25 0.51
50 0.80
100 0.98
150 1.00
````` ::: ::: ## One-factor between-subject design with a continuous predictor This design is similar to the one-way ANOVA but it incorporates a covariate, in what is known as an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). It is used to compare the means of an outcome across two or more groups while controlling for the influence of other variables, called covariates. In other words, ANCOVA allows researchers to compare adjusted group means, accounting for the variability associated with the covariate. Including a covariate improves the precision of group comparisons by explaining part of the error variance and thus increasing power. Suppose a researcher hypothesizes that heart rate differs between individuals who did and did not consume alcohol the previous night. To control for the potential influence of physical fitness, the researcher includes "physical fitness" as a covariate. In this case: 1) heart rate is the primary outcome, 2) alcohol intake (yes or no) is the independent grouping variable, and 3) physical fitness (hours of physical activity per week) is the covariate. By including physical fitness as a covariate, the researcher can control for its influence and better isolate the effect of alcohol consumption on heart rate. Let's define the parameters of the simulation and plot the pattern of means: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Set parameters nsims <- 1000 # number of simulations sample_size <- c(50, 100, 150, 200, 250) # sample size mu1 <- 64 # mean heart rate for alcohol group mu2 <- 60 # mean heart rate for non-alcohol group sd <- 10 # SD for both groups mu3 <- 5 # mean hours of exercise (covariate) sd3 <- 3 # SD of the covariate rho <- 0.8 # correlation between heart rate and exercise alpha_level <- 0.05 # Sample size per group for the illustration n <- 50 df <- sim_design( between = list(group = c("alcohol", "noalcohol")), mu = list(alcohol = mu1, noalcohol = mu2), sd = sd, n = n, plot = TRUE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06_chapter_files/figure-html/chunk_62-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Let's run the simulations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Ensure reproducibility set.seed(050990) # Power simulation function simulate_power <- function(n) { group <- factor(rep(c("noalcohol", "alcohol"), each = n), levels = c("noalcohol", "alcohol")) group_effect <- ifelse(group == "alcohol", mu1, mu2) p_values <- replicate(nsims, { # Residual heart rate without a group effect residual <- rnorm(2 * n, mean = 0, sd = sd) # Covariate correlated with the residuals but not with group membership exercise <- mu3 + sd3 * (rho * residual / sd + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(2 * n)) y <- group_effect + residual summary(lm(y ~ group + exercise))$coefficients["groupalcohol", "Pr(>|t|)"] }) mean(p_values < alpha_level) } # Run function for all sample sizes power_results <- tibble( n = sample_size, power = map_dbl(sample_size, simulate_power) ) # Return proportion of significant p-values power_results |> kable(digits = 2) |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
n power
50 0.9
100 1.0
150 1.0
200 1.0
250 1.0
````` ::: :::
